hop.note: The owner's words land in Claude Code's own session transcript the instant the turn is submitted -- there is no separate 'arrival' write to wait for. A dedicated hook (.claude/hooks/prompt-relay.mjs) exists on disk to log arrival separately but is not wired into settings.json today, so this hop is inferred to be near-zero rather than independently measured.

Measured as the gap between the owner's turn timestamp in the session transcript (ae22125c-...jsonl) and the fast assistant's own 'say.mjs heard' command a few seconds later. That one command writes both the dev-bar echo and the board.jsonl card in a single call, confirmed by the next hop's near-zero gap, so 'echoed' and 'carded' are the same real-world moment, not two.

40 of 48 pairs land at exactly the same second: the card in board.jsonl and the chat line in the mastermind's inbox are written by the same command. 8 pairs show a gap up to 115s, but that is very likely this audit's own nearest-timestamp matching picking the wrong neighbor when two owner messages arrived close together, not a real delay -- say.mjs has no code path that would separate these two writes in time.

Measured as the first mastermind log/agent/decision line after a chat line and before the owner's next one, so a burst of quick messages (19 of 53) has no clean window and is excluded rather than mismatched to the wrong pickup. This number comes from a session where the mastermind was live and conversational; see the page for why the real number can be much worse when the mastermind is running on its own timer instead.

Measured directly from the mastermind's own task log by pairing each agent's dispatch line with that same agent's landing line (matched by task name, the same convention the dashboard itself uses). This is mostly real work -- an agent reading files, writing code, and checking it -- not idle waiting.

A second, cruder check: for each owner message, the very next piece of finished work to land anywhere on the board, no matter which request caused it. This is higher than summing the five stages above (about 29 minutes) because it also captures queueing -- a message that arrives while three other things are already being built has to wait for the whole line, which is exactly the complaint 'a one-line change should never queue.' Treat this as an upper bound illustrating the queueing effect, not a clean per-message measurement, since 13 of 53 messages could not be paired to a landing within 90 minutes and were dropped rather than guessed at.
